contributions.headingText: Squamous papilloma (SP) and squamous papillomatosis are benign exophytic-papillary squamous epithelial neoplasms usually with low-risk HPV.

8052/0 Squamous papilloma of the larynx

8060/0 Squamous papillomatosis of the larynx

2F00.Y & XH50T2 Other specified benign neoplasm of middle ear or respiratory system & Squamous cell papilloma, NOS

2E90 & XH50T2 Benign neoplasm of lip, oral cavity, or pharynx & Squamous cell papilloma, NOS

Acceptable: recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP); laryngeal papillomatosis; squamous cell papilloma.

 

Not recommended: juvenile papillomatosis; adult papillomatosis.

The distribution of squamous papillomatosis follows a predictable pattern, with the tumours occurring at sites where ciliated epithelium and squamous epithelium are juxtaposed. Any oral mucosal site may be affected, but solitary lesions have a predilection for the palatal complex and oral tongue {6154913; 25598510}. Within the larynx, where multifocal disease is common, the vocal cords and ventricles are most frequently affected, followed by the false cords, epiglottis, subglottic area, hypopharynx, and nasopharynx. Lower respiratory tract extension is rare (occurring in 1–3% of cases), often associated with high mortality {18281102}.

A painless soft nodule with pink or white finger-like fronds or a pebbly, cauliflower-like surface and pedunculated base are the characteristic findings for SP {25598510}. There is clinical overlap with solitary verruca vulgaris and condyloma acuminatum. Laryngeal tumours are associated with symptoms of progressive hoarseness, stridor, chronic cough, and dysphagia.

SP is the most common benign epithelial tumour of the larynx and oral cavity in children {6154913; 25598510}. Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP) is a rare disease that occurs in children and adults. The projected annual estimates of RRP incidence are 4.3 cases per 100 000 children and approximately 1.8 cases per 100 000 adults {25999724; 18496162}. There is a bimodal age distribution, with the first peak occurring at < 5 years of age (juvenile cases) and the second peak at 20–40 years (adult cases) {25999724; 23204170}. RRP is more common in children than in adults and is the most aggressive form of SP, with 25% of cases arising during infancy {12975271; 15514560}. There is no sex predilection in children. Although the disease is rare, morbidity is notoriously high, because it compromises functions such as vocalization, swallowing, and breathing {15514560; 18281102}.

HPV6 and HPV11 (identified in 90% of cases) are the genotypes most frequently associated with RRP and solitary oral SP {15514560; 30693456}, with a minority of RRP cases (4–5%) showing coinfection. Other HPV genotypes (e.g. 16, 31, 33, 35, and 39) are found in a minority of cases (3–4%) {15514560}. The modes of HPV transmission include non-sexual contact, maternal contact (direct or indirect), and sexual contact {21600804}. Most neonatal HPV infection occurs by vertical transmission at birth {20553530}. A triad of factors (first-born child, vaginal delivery, and maternal age < 20 years) correlates with RRP in children {1309932}. An active maternal genital HPV infection at the time of delivery increases exposure to a significant viral load, with a high risk of transmitting infection. Caesarean section provides a lower risk of transmission but is not completely protective against infection {30693456; 20553530}.

HPVs are double-stranded DNA viruses, differentiated by the genetic sequence of the outer capsid protein L1. The virions replicate within the nuclei of infected host cells {15187189}. More than 40 types affect mucosal epithelium, separated into non-oncogenic types (e.g. HPV6 and HPV11) and oncogenic types (e.g. HPV16 and HPV18). Viral infection occurs at the basal epithelium, frequently in zones of the body lined by squamous epithelium with a squamocolumnar transition. The transcripts initiated at major viral promoter sites in oncogenic types are not seen in non-oncogenic types.
A sessile or pedunculated nodule with a bosselated, papillary surface is characteristic.

SPs are exophytic-verrucous, composed of an arborizing fibrovascular network covered by squamous epithelium ranging from non-keratinized to showing varying degrees of keratinization. Koilocytic atypia (crenated nucleus, perinuclear halo, prominent cell borders) may be seen, but epithelial dysplasia is infrequently observed and should be reported if present. Mitoses may be increased in traumatized or inflamed lesions. In RRP, premature keratinization of individual epithelial cells contributes to a disorganized appearance. The distribution of RRP follows a predictable pattern, occurring where ciliated and squamous epithelium is juxtaposed.

Specific HPV genotyping is not diagnostically required {25419846}, but in situ hybridization can distinguish between episomal or integrated patterns {25419846}. Papilloma recurrence in paediatric patients may be more attributable to HPV integration {22052184}.

Essential: exophytic multilayered benign squamous cell proliferation; central fibrovascular cores supporting epithelial proliferation.

Desirable: isolated koilocytes; low-risk HPV type (in selected cases).

Most oral and oropharyngeal SPs persist for years without increasing in size or dissemination, with a minimal risk of recurrence (2%) {25598510}. The clinical course of RRP, however, is unpredictable and ranges from complete remission, to relatively stable lesions, to an aggressive clinical course of rapid, progressive recurrences associated with potentially life-threatening respiratory obstruction {18496162; 20553530; 2429122}. Children diagnosed at < 3 years of age are 3.6 times as likely as children diagnosed at an older age to have more than four surgeries per year {12975271; 25419846}. HPV11 is more closely associated with a younger age at diagnosis and sometimes an aggressive clinical course {15514560}. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis found that the HPV vaccine significantly reduced the number of surgical procedures and increased the time between surgeries in both children and adults {30358875}, with further vaccine effects still to be determined {25999724}. Oral SPs do not undergo malignant transformation, but there is a 1–4% rate of malignant transformation of RRP into squamous cell carcinoma, especially in the setting of irradiation, smoking, or another promoter {18496162; 23641321; 21526134; 2491876}.
